plan: [ This two-stage auction is strategically equivalent to a second-price auction: highest bid wins and pays the second-highest bid (the clock at the rival’s exit). With independent private values and risk neutrality, bidding one’s true value is a dominant strategy. Shading risks losing profitable wins; overbidding risks paying above value. Ties are random, giving no gain from small deviations. Therefore, I should bid exactly my value to maximize expected profit. My value this round is $31. ]

[ In a second-price auction (equivalent to this two-stage format), bidding your true value is a weakly dominant strategy regardless of others’ strategies. This maximizes expected profit without needing to infer others’ behavior, especially with no past rounds to learn from. With value 22, bidding 22 ensures: - If highest competing bid < 22, I win and pay that bid, yielding nonnegative profit equal to 22 − price. - If any competitor bids ≥ 22, I lose and pay nothing, avoiding negative profit. Tie at 22 is broken randomly, which is optimal given no better alternative. ]

[ This is strategically equivalent to a 3-bidder second-price auction via precommitted exit prices. The dominant strategy is to bid my true value: it maximizes expected profit by winning exactly when my value is the highest and paying the second-highest value. Underbidding risks losing profitable auctions; overbidding risks winning and paying above my value. With uniform independent values and tie-breaking random, truth-telling is optimal even without history. Therefore, I bid $40.0 (within $0.1 increments). ]
